<x_0.1914><y_0.0297>we doubt the truths of fuch facts, we mult at least ac- knowledge their probability, fince we meet every day with a number of familiar examples. When we fee a chefs-player to deeply immersed in thought as to be in a manner loft to his outward fenêes, thould we not ima- gine him to be wholly engroffed with the care of his own private affairs, or of the public went? but the ob- jest of all this profound meditation is the pleasure of ex- ercifing the mind by the movement of a piece of ivory. From this exercise of the mind also writes the pleasure we fometimes take in refined and delicate fentiments, which, after the manner of Virgil's thepherds, (Et fugit ad fulicer, fed fe cupit ante videri), are fometimes artfully concealed, but fo as to afford us the pleasure of difcovering them \*."<x_0.9795><y_0.2273><class_Text>

<x_0.0488><y_0.2133>_Theorie del Sentiments agréable._<x_0.1963><y_0.2602><class_Caption>

<x_0.1895><y_0.225>From home of the foregoing remarks we alfo fee that nature points out to us the superiority and excellence of our mental faculties, thus fuggetting to us that we ought to cultivate them moft, as being our better and our no-bler part, to the cultivation of which that of our fenfi-tive faculties thould be merely fubfervient. But, although our pleafures are thus by nature rendered in a great degree independent of ourselves, fill we have it in our power to make them all more durable; by varying and mixing them with one another, or by interpo-ling between those that are very agreeable others that are less pleading, fo as that no individual pleasure shall be in excels.<x_0.9785><y_0.3937><class_Text>

<x_0.1855><y_0.393>Befides the circumstances already noticed, there are others of a very different kind, which have alfo confi-derable influence on the pleafures of the fenêes ; fuch as different conditions of the whole body, particularly of the nerves, or of certain organs or functions, to which functions fome organs of fenês, and perhaps even the fenfation of thefe, are in a great measure fubfervient. This is one of the causes why many pleafures, which we cultivate with all our might, cannot be immortal. If a person be thirty, fpring water is nectar to him ; if hungry, any kind of food is agreeable, even the fmell of food is grateful. To a man in a heat, or in a fever, cold is pleating ; and to one in a cold fit nothing is fo agreeable as heat. To thefe fame perfons, at other times, fo far are thefe things from being agreeable, that they are often diliguing. The molt decided glutton cannot always relish a fumptuous feaft.<x_0.9775><y_0.6148><class_Text>

<x_0.1836><y_0.6141>Befides the fenfations excited by external objects, there are others alfo which cause pain and pleasure. If the action of the muticles be frong, easy, and cheerful, and not continued fo as to fatigue us, it causes pleasure. On the contrary, when this action is attended with a fenêe of lifllethiefs, latitude, difficulty, and debility, it can- fes pain more or lefs. In fine, various flates and affections of the mind, fuch as the exercife of memory, imagination, and judgement, nearly for familiar reafons, are fometimes painful, at other times agreeable. " Animi affectus, qui modici grate excitant, vehementes, aut graves et dinturni, hujus pariter ac corporis vires frangunt ; hominem interdum flatim extinguunt, fe-pius longa valetudine macerant. Somni etiam, quo ud exhauflas vires reficiendas egemus, excerflus, vel de-fectus, et animo et corpori nocet."-- Defidia, five animi five corporis, utriufque vires languefount: ni-nia exercitatione haud minus lieduntur.
